title: The Housing Market is Broken: Why Homes Are Unaffordable & What It Takes to Fix It | The Weekly Wrap
summary: Eisman argues that mortgage lock-in, constrained local supply and rising ownership costs explain housing’s weakness despite better-run builders. He distinguishes builders from companies exposed to existing-home transactions and favors supply reforms over buyer subsidies. FHFA loan-level research supports the lock-in mechanism; other quantitative and causal claims need matched evidence. He also discusses AI risks to software franchises, skepticism about crypto valuation and ETF structure. His practical fund comparison is mostly sound, but passive portfolios do change with their indices and not every mutual fund is actively managed.
assessment: Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.
speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman is the sole substantive speaker; viewer questions are distinguished from his responses.
framework_points: Separate new-home and existing-home transaction exposure.
Compare earnings deterioration with stock expectations before assuming fundamentals are improving.
Model mortgage payments explicitly and distinguish liquidity lock-in from construction constraints.
Compare demand subsidies with supply elasticity.
Evaluate fund structure, costs and taxes separately from manager skill.
tools_and_charts: Builder and building-product company EPS and share-return tables
Zelman entry-level affordability index including taxes and insurance
Mortgage rate distribution, public builder market share and housing shortage estimates
ETF fees, trading, disclosure and in-kind redemption
transcript_cautions: He corrects an earlier electricity-unit error from terawatts to terawatt-hours.
The mortgage example assumes full financing and excludes taxes and insurance.
Historical and current fund terminology is simplified; mutual fund is a legal structure, not a synonym for active management.

evidence.title: The Lock-In Effect of Rising Mortgage Rates, Working Paper 24-03
evidence.finding: Primary loan-level research estimates higher market rates relative to existing loans reduce sale probability. Original abstract estimates 1.33 million prevented sales in 2022Q2-2023Q4 and upward price pressure from reduced supply. Estimates support the mechanism, not every December 2025 market statistic.

claims.claim: On a fully financed $400,000 thirty-year mortgage, moving from four to 6.25 percent raises principal-and-interest payments from about $1,900 to $2,500.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Recalculate standard fixed-rate amortization for the stated assumptions.
claims.reason: Using payment=P*r/(1-(1+r)^(-360)) gives approximately $1,910 and $2,463 at monthly rates 0.04/12 and 0.0625/12. Rounded illustrative payments are reasonable; taxes, insurance and down payment are excluded.

claims.claim: Passive ETFs track a specified index at generally low fees, while active funds pay managers to select securities.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect the relevant index methodology and fund prospectus rather than treating legal structure as strategy.
claims.reason: SEC confirms index-tracking and active ETF strategies. The accompanying claim that passive portfolios never change is too absolute: tracking a changing index requires portfolio changes. Mutual funds can also be passive.

evidence.title: Updated investor bulletin on exchange-traded funds
evidence.finding: Retail ETF shares trade in secondary markets. Authorized participants create/redeem large units, typically with in-kind baskets. ETF selling therefore need not mechanically cause an equivalent cash sale by the fund; index and ETF flow effects require separate analysis.

claims.next_check: Obtain primary evidence matching the stated metric, period and conditions before assigning an outcome grade.

claims.claim: ETFs trade throughout the day, unlike mutual funds’ once-daily order processing, and in-kind transactions can improve tax efficiency and reduce costs.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare all-in costs and after-tax returns for matched strategies.
claims.reason: SEC confirms intraday exchange trading, potential lower costs and fewer capital-gain distributions from in-kind exchanges. These are structural tendencies, subject to spreads, premiums and individual fund design.
